name: New Orleans
info: New Orleans is a city on the Mississippi River in Louisiana, founded by the French in 1718, held by Spain and then by the United States from 1803, and for a time the largest port and slave market of the American South.

facts.founded: In early 1718 by the French, as La Nouvelle-Orléans, under the Louisiana governor Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, on land traditionally inhabited by the Chitimacha people.
facts.where: On the Mississippi River in its delta, south of Lake Pontchartrain and about 105 miles (169 km) upriver from the Gulf of Mexico, in Louisiana, United States.
facts.known: A French colonial capital on a river bend; the largest slave market in the United States; the Battle of New Orleans in 1815; a cotton port; Creole culture and the birthplace of jazz; Plessy v. Ferguson; Hurricane Katrina in 2005
facts.today: New Orleans is the most populous city of Louisiana and a consolidated city-parish, coextensive with Orleans Parish.

t: The French founded New Orleans in 1718 on a natural levee beside a portage used by Native Americans, and it passed to Spain in 1763, briefly back to France, and to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

Cotton, sugar and a large domestic slave trade made it the wealthiest and third most populous city in the United States by 1840, while free people of color, Creoles, Irish, Germans and others gave it a mixed population and culture.
Fires, yellow fever, floods and hurricanes struck the city repeatedly, and in 2005 the failure of its levees in Hurricane Katrina flooded about 80 percent of it.
dyk: The Choctaw name for the area, Bulbancha, has been translated as "place of many tongues". Congo Square was a place where enslaved people were allowed to gather in public and play their native music.
ev: The French found La Nouvelle-Orléans under Bienville
France cedes the colony west of the Mississippi and New Orleans to Spain
The Great New Orleans Fire destroys 856 buildings
Napoleon sells Louisiana to the United States and New Orleans passes to American rule
Andrew Jackson's forces defeat the British at the Battle of New Orleans
A Union fleet takes the city after passing Forts Jackson and St. Philip
The Supreme Court decides Plessy v. Ferguson, a case begun in New Orleans
Hurricane Katrina and the failure of the levees flood most of the city

sections.origins:
New Orleans stands on the banks of the Mississippi River in the Mississippi River Delta, south of Lake Pontchartrain. The land was formed around 2200 BCE, when the river deposited silt and created the delta region. Archaeological evidence shows settlement in the area dating back to at least 400 CE, and peoples of the Mississippian culture built mounds and earthworks there. Later Native Americans created a portage between the headwaters of Bayou St. John and the Mississippi, and since the bayou flowed into Lake Pontchartrain this became an important trade route. Bulbancha, a Choctaw name for the area, translates as "place of many tongues", and it was a trading hub for thousands of years.

French explorers, fur trappers and traders arrived by the 1690s, some settling among a Native American village of thatched huts along the bayou. In 1701 the French built a small fort, St. Jean, at the mouth of the bayou on a large shell midden of the Marksville culture. Land grants were given to settlers from Mobile in 1708, but most left within two years after they failed to grow wheat. New Orleans itself was founded in early 1718 by the French, under Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, on land traditionally inhabited by the Chitimacha people. Bienville chose relatively high ground on a natural levee at a sharp bend of the flood-prone river, on the site of an abandoned Quinipissa village, beside the portage to Lake Pontchartrain. The city was named for Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, regent of France.
sections.growth:
The French intended New Orleans to be an important colonial city. John Law's private bank and financing scheme increased the colonial population, but the investment bubble burst at the end of 1720 and the Mississippi Company collapsed. In 1721 the priest Charlevoix described a place of a hundred wretched hovels in a malarious wet thicket. In 1722 it replaced Biloxi as the capital of French Louisiana. Its position made it the gateway for goods moving between the interior of North America and the Atlantic world.

Two fires under Spanish rule were followed by rebuilding in brick, and the commerce of the Mississippi grew. The Carondelet Canal to Lake Pontchartrain opened in 1794, and the sugar industry was put on a firm basis in 1795 and 1796. A census of 1805 counted 8,500 people, though the true figure was thought to be about 10,000. The population doubled in the 1830s, and by 1840 the city had about 102,000 people and was the wealthiest and third most populous in the United States, the largest away from the Atlantic seaboard and the largest in the South. It exported most of the nation's cotton, and a branch of the United States Mint opened there in 1838. By 1860 it had nearly 170,000 people and was the third-largest American port by import tonnage.

Its relative importance declined from the mid-19th century as railways and highways reduced river traffic. The 1970 census recorded the first absolute fall in population since 1803, after a peak of 627,525 recorded before 1960.
sections.rulers:
New Orleans was under the Kingdom of France from its founding. It was the capital of French Louisiana from 1722, and in 1763, after Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War, France ceded the colony west of the Mississippi, with the city, to the Spanish Empire, as a secret provision of the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau confirmed by the Treaty of Paris. No Spanish governor arrived until 1766. In 1768 French and German settlers forced him to flee in a bloodless rebellion; a year later Spain reasserted control, executed five ringleaders, sent five plotters to prison in Cuba and formally instituted Spanish law.

Spain and France signed the secret Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800, returning Louisiana to France. Napoleon sold it to the United States in April 1803, and the prefect Pierre Clément de Laussat took control for France on 30 November and handed it to the United States on 20 December 1803, and created the city's first council. In 1836 the city was divided into three municipalities. The city joined the Confederacy in 1861 and was taken by Union forces in April 1862, when General Benjamin Butler became military governor. During Reconstruction Louisiana was in the Fifth Military District and was readmitted to the Union in 1868 with a constitution granting universal male suffrage. On 14 September 1874 the White League defeated the integrated Republican police in a battle in the French Quarter and on Canal Street; federal troops restored the Republican government three days later, and after their withdrawal in 1877 the Democrats held control of the state and city.
sections.life:
From early days the city had a polyglot population and a mixture of cultures. Spanish rule brought immigrants from Spain, the Canary Islands and elsewhere in the Atlantic world, and Filipinos began settling in the region from the 1760s. Refugees from the Haitian Revolution, white people and free people of color, arrived between 1791 and 1810, many bringing enslaved people; the migration of 1809 brought 2,731 whites, 3,102 free people of African descent and 3,226 enslaved people, doubling the city's French-speaking population, and the city became 63 percent black. Free people of color formed an artisan and professional class, and Irish, German and other immigrants followed. Sephardic Jews formed the first Jewish congregation in the 1830s. One report of 1902 said a quarter of the city spoke French daily.

Slavery was central to the city's economy. Enslaved Africans were arriving in significant numbers by the early 1720s, and the Code Noir of 1724 set harsh laws over their lives. After the United States ended the international slave trade in 1808 New Orleans housed the largest slave market in the country, and two-thirds of the more than one million enslaved people moved in the domestic trade went to the Deep South. In the 1840s about 50 companies sold people, and some whites went to the markets, such as the St. Louis Hotel Slave Market and the New Orleans Exchange, for entertainment. There was great demand for "fancy girls", young women kept as concubines. An Afro-Creole culture developed, with Louisiana Voodoo and Louisiana Creole.
sections.crises:
A hurricane in September 1722 blew down most of the city's buildings. On Good Friday, 21 March 1788, a fire destroyed 856 buildings, and another in December 1794 destroyed 212. Yellow fever threatened the city from 1817 to 1905, and the worst epidemic, in 1853, killed about 8,000 people; epidemics killed over 150,000 residents in the 19th century. A levee breach upriver on 3 May 1849 left 12,000 people homeless.

In January 1811 hundreds of enslaved people on plantations upriver rose in the German Coast Uprising and marched toward the city, killing two white men. Militia and United States forces put it down; ninety-five black people were killed in confrontations and in executions after local tribunals, and over two weeks planters and officials executed 44 more captured insurgents, displaying their bodies, and the heads of some, as a warning. In 1891 a mob stormed the jail after Italian Americans tried for the shooting of the police chief were acquitted and lynched eleven of them.

On 29 August 2005 Hurricane Katrina made landfall near the city. The mayor ordered the first mandatory evacuation in its history, and an estimated 1 million people left Greater New Orleans, though some 20 percent of residents remained, many sheltering in the Superdome. Levees on four canals were breached and as much as 80 percent of the city flooded, with water up to 25 feet (7.6 m) deep in places. More than 1,500 deaths were recorded in Louisiana, most in New Orleans. The city population fell from an estimate of 454,865 before the storm to 223,000 in July 2006.
sections.legacy:
The street grid ordered by Bienville survives in the French Quarter. Nearly all the surviving 18th-century architecture there dates from the Spanish period, including St. Louis Cathedral, the Cabildo and the Presbytere, built after the fires. In the early 20th century the blending of European instruments with African rhythms produced jazz, and brass bands, jazz funerals and Mardi Gras remain part of the city's life, alongside a Creole cuisine and a distinctive dialect.

The city was also a centre of the struggle over civil rights. Free people of color organised the Comité des Citoyens and recruited Homer Plessy to test Louisiana's Separate Car Act, and the Supreme Court's ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 upheld "separate but equal" accommodations. In the 20th century the Southern Christian Leadership Conference was founded there, and Ruby Bridges integrated William Frantz Elementary School in 1960. A monument to the White League's Battle of Liberty Place was removed in 2017. During the Second World War the Higgins boats were developed and built in the city.

New Orleans is today the most populous city in Louisiana, a consolidated city-parish coextensive with Orleans Parish, with 383,997 people at the 2020 census. Half of the city lies at or below mean sea level, and parts of it are sinking. Levees and drainage pumps protect it, and its port remains a major one.

summary: New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718 on the Mississippi, passed to Spain and then to the United States in 1803, and grew into a cotton port and the largest slave market in the country. Fires, epidemics and hurricanes struck it, most severely Katrina in 2005.
references: Jay Gitlin, The Bourgeois Frontier: French Towns, French Traders, and American Expansion (Yale University Press, 2009)
notes: FOUNDING: main article says land traditionally inhabited by the Chitimacha and 'spring of 1718'; history article says 'early 1718' and an abandoned Quinipissa village on the site, and a Native American village of thatched huts on the bayou in the 1690s. I gave both, attributing each.

NATIVE HABITATION: history article says Native Americans inhabited the area 'about 1300 years' before Europeans and also settlement 'at least 400 C.E.'; the two do not fit together, so I kept only 400 CE.
BULBANCHA: history gives 'place of many tongues'; main article gives 'land of many tongues' and says the name may refer to the river. I used 'place of many tongues' (facts/dyk and origins).

CESSION DATES: main article gives the French period as 1718-1762 and the Spanish period as 1762-1801 in its infobox; history article gives 1718-1763 and 1763-1802, and the text gives 1763 (Treaty of Paris). I used 1763 and 1800/1803.

CAPITAL OF LOUISIANA: history article says the city again served as state capital 'from 1865 to 1880' and elsewhere '1864-1882'; I left those years out. 1849 Baton Rouge replaced it (stated; I did not state it in the text).

KATRINA DEATHS: main lead says 'more than 1,300 people', its history section says 'more than 1,500 people were recorded as having died in Louisiana, most in New Orleans, while others remain unaccounted for'; history article says 1,836 total, 1,577 in Louisiana. I used only 'more than 1,500 recorded in Louisiana'. Evacuation: history says an estimated 600,000 evacuated on 29 August (apparently a stale passage) and 1 million before the storm; I used 1 million.

POPULATION: main article has 383,997 (lead) and also 383,997/383,997 in demographics. July 2006 estimate 223,000 (main) vs 273,000 in August 2007 (history); I used 223,000 and 454,865 (last estimate before Katrina, 1 July 2005). Peak 627,525 is 'prior to 1960'; main says the population reached its historic peak in 1960.

GERMAN COAST UPRISING: history gives 64 to 125 marching, 200 to 500 in some accounts, and 95 black people killed plus 44 more executed; main says about 500. I omitted the number of participants and kept the death figures. I read 'ninety-five' as killed in confrontations and executions after tribunals, and the 44 as additional, as the history article words it.

SPANISH REBELLION 1768: the main article says residents sent a delegation to France; history says French and German settlers forced the governor to flee. Both used loosely; I gave the history article's account.

FIRST/LARGEST: 'third most populous in 1840' (both articles); main also says fifth-largest in 1860. I kept 'nearly 170,000' and 'third-largest port by import tonnage' for 1860 and did not state a rank for 1860.

CONGO SQUARE: the article says New Orleans was 'the only North American city to have allowed slaves to gather in public and play their native music'; the dyk word 'was said to be' hedges it, since it is an assertion of the article, not a hedged one. Editor may prefer to state it plainly.

NEW ORLEANS 1815: casualty figures for the battle are in the history article (2,000 of 9,000 British troops); omitted for space, and the main article gives 11,000 for the British force, which conflicts with the 9,000 engaged (different measures).

Left out as tourism, sports, rankings, airports or the present government: the Saints, Super Bowls, convention business, the 2025 truck attack and National Guard deployment, Mardi Gras detail, the Storyville district, the World's Fairs, and the 2005 post-Katrina investigation findings on the levee design and its builders (the history article names the Army Corps of Engineers, contractors and the Levee Board; I left that attribution out to avoid giving a verdict on any government body, but the editor may want a neutral sentence from the ASCE report quoted in the main article).

Katrina flooding cause: main says the failure of the 'federal flood protection system'; history says four canals breached with surge funnelled via the Mississippi River Gulf Outlet; I wrote only that levees on four canals were breached.
Higgins boats: both the history article and my text say they were developed and built in the city; 'Eisenhower proclaimed them vital' was left out.
